data.description: Coordinate the operator and banking sides

UAE telecom licence rules address planned service interruptions but do not explicitly require operators to manage or roll back automated fraud-model changes that cause widespread denial of legitimate SIM-replacement requests.
There is no excerpted UAE rule requiring OpCo to notify TDRA after an unplanned service-impacting change occurs; the only notification duty found is advance notice for planned interruptions.
The UAE PDPL excerpts do not specify a time limit within which OpCo must notify the Bureau of a personal data breach; the relevant excerpt only lists actions to be taken in the event of a breach.

The UAE telecom excerpts provided do not impose explicit SIM replacement, SIM-swap or customer authentication obligations on mobile operators for roaming customers; they only contain interruption notification duties.

The provided UAE telecom licence excerpt specifies notice for planned interruptions but does not state a deadline for notifying the TDRA and customers of an unplanned automated fraud-control service interruption like this one.

The UAE consumer protection framework as retrieved does not explicitly require a licensee to provide a human review path or prompt remediation when automated fraud controls erroneously refuse legitimate SIM replacement requests, leaving affected roaming and prepaid users without service.

The incident exposes that the UAE PDPL excerpts contain a data subject right to information about automated decisions but no explicit obligation for a controller to provide a human review or appeal path when automated processing refuses a service.

The UAE regulatory framework does not explicitly require licensees to provide a human review or appeal mechanism for automated SIM replacement refusals or to explain automated decisions to affected customers.
UAE-PDPL excerpts recognise a data subject right to receive information about automated decisions, but they do not provide an explicit right to contest such decisions or to obtain human intervention.
Enforcement ownership for private-sector PDPL complaints is unclear because no supervisory authority has been unambiguously designated and the implementing regulations have not been issued.
UAE has no rule requiring a human review path for customers whose legitimate SIM replacement requests are refused by fraud-control automation, leaving them without remedy.
OpCo's fraud model v2 operated without a human review path for refused SIM replacement requests, exposing a gap between the PDPL human-review requirement and operational implementation.
The retrieved UAE rules do not require a human review path for automated fraud-model refusals; the closest duty is the DPIA requirement under UAE-PDPL#0066.
No retrieved UAE rule expressly requires an operator to provide human review or an appeal path when an automated SIM replacement request is refused.
The UAE PDPL lacks an explicit, enforceable right to human review or appeal of automated decisions; it only provides a right to receive information about automated processing.
No UAE telecom-specific rule requires a mobile operator to provide a human review path when an automated fraud model refuses a SIM replacement request.

The incident exposed a policy gap: the provided UAE data protection excerpts contain no explicit requirement for a human review path when automated fraud-refusal decisions block legitimate SIM-replacement requests.

The provided UAE data protection excerpts require an impact assessment and DPO coordination, but they do not require prior consultation with the UAE data protection authority before high-risk processing such as the fraud model v2 deployment.
No retrieved UAE rule requires OpCo to provide a human review path or appeal mechanism for automated SIM replacement refusals.
The retrieved UAE excerpts do not identify a UAE instrument that sets authentication requirements for SIM-swap requests; a court decision refers to identification protocol without naming it.
No retrieved UAE rule sets a deadline for restoring legitimate SIM replacement processing or establishing human review after refusals began at 08:00.

The PDPL gives data subjects a right to receive information about decisions made based on automated processing, but the excerpts contain no rule requiring a human review or appeal path when an automated decision refuses a service such as SIM replacement.

The PDPL requires a controller to notify the Bureau of a personal data breach or violation within a period set by the Executive Regulations, but the Decree-Law quoted here states no explicit hours or days; therefore no statutory deadline is visible to the Bureau in this incident.

The UAE consumer protection framework in the excerpts defaults two-factor authentication to OTP and does not require a human review path or alternative authentication when a SIM replacement is refused, leaving prepaid and roaming bank customers locked out.
